newsitem.title: USA: UCLA economists see Fed tightening over next year.
newsitem.headline: UCLA economists see Fed tightening over next year.

text.p: Economists at the University of California at Los Angeles on Wednesday expect the Federal Reserve Bank to push interest rates higher during the next 12 months to keep the U.S. economy from expanding too rapidly.

According to the university's quarterly economic forecast, the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets U.S. monetary policy, will likely raise its Fed Funds target rate by 150 basis points to seven percent over the next 12 months from the current 5.50 percent. The Fed Funds rate, the interest rate U.S. banks charge each other on overnight loans, is widely regarded as a key indicator of U.S. interest rates.
The Federal Reserve last moved to raise rates in March when it increased its Fed Funds target by 25 basis points. Since then, it has made no policy changes.

But even though inflation is not seen as a threat now, it could become a problem, and the Fed needs to raise interest rates steadily over the next 12 months to maintain control, the UCLA economists said.

"If you don't want the economy to get overheated, which usually leads to inflation, then the only choice you have as a monetary policy-maker is to use the Federal Funds rate to put the brakes on," said Rajeev Dhawan, one of the authors of the forecast.
Slowing annual real gross domestic product (GDP) growth to about one percent in the first half of 1998 would ensure a soft landing for the economy and avert recession, the report said.
Without a preemptive tightening of monetary policy, inflation could accelerate to five percent by the end of the century, the economists said.
The report said the current inflation rate is deceptively low because of reduced oil prices.
While the consumer price index (CPI) has edged up only 0.1 percent in each of the past three months, the increase was greater when the volatile food and energy components.

On Tuesday, the Labor Department reported the CPI overall rose 0.1 percent in May. Excluding food and energy, the so-called core CPI was up 0.2 percent. Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2 percent increase in both the overall and core rates for May.

UCLA economists forecast inflation, excluding volatile food and energy components, would accelerate to 2.9 percent this year, step up to 3.5 percent in 1998 and then drop back to about 2.6 percent in 2000.

They said a tighter monetary policy would yield GDP growth of 1.8 percent in 1998 and about 2.5 percent in 1999 and 2000, allowing U.S. unemployment rates to rise to about 5.6 percent in 1998 and 5.8 percent in 1999 and 2000.
Meanwhile, corporate profits are expected to rise 11.2 percent in 1997 before dropping 1.7 percent in 1998.
